(CNN)  -- Houston, Texas, had a record high temperature Wednesday as a heat wave continues to grip the nation's midsection, the National Weather Service said Thursday. A woman tries to beat Houston's record heat by lying on a bench in the shade. The city sweltered with a high temperature of 104 degrees Wednesday, a record high for June 24, forecasters said. The previous record high for the date was 99 degrees, set in 1980. The previous record high measured for the month of June in Houston was 103 degrees, set on June 30, 1980, and June 18, 1934. Heat indices, a combination of temperature and humidity, are breaking the 110-degree mark in many cities. Forecasters predicted a high near 100 for Houston on Thursday, but the temperature could rise into the triple digits in outlying areas, said CNN meteorologist Reynolds Wolf. I don't do much shopping, that's for sure." Betty Dante added, "It is very hot outside. ... I think as you get older, you feel the heat more." In southwest Houston, Leticia Alvarado is profiting from the heat. The unemployed Houstonian has been running along the median on Hillcroft Street at Bellaire Boulevard for seven weeks. She is selling water for $1 a bottle. "It's hot, too hot," she told the station. Other cities also were sweltering. New Iberia, Louisiana, had a temperature Wednesday of 102, which broke the record of 97 in 2005. An excessive heat warning was issued for St. Louis, Missouri, on Thursday through 7 p.m. CT Saturday. Forecasters predicted a high near 96. Cloud cover was expected to make temperatures there a little cooler Thursday, but the weather service warned, "A hot and humid air mass remains over the area which will continue to control weather over the region through Saturday." Afternoon and early evening heat index readings of 100 to 110 were expected in the Missouri city every day through Saturday. Young children, the elderly and people with chronic sicknesses were advised to stay inside if possible. The heat wave that began last week was being fed by a high pressure system north of Texas . According to the **National Weather Service office in Houston/Galveston**, temperatures at **George Bush Intercontinental Airport**, Houston’s official climate observation site, climbed into record territory this week, with afternoon highs reaching or nearing the city’s all-time marks. The weather service reported heat index values — what the temperature feels like when humidity is factored in — soaring above **110 degrees** in parts of the metro area.

The NWS issued **heat advisories and excessive heat warnings** for much of Southeast Texas, including Harris, Fort Bend, Brazoria, Galveston, Montgomery and Liberty counties. Forecasters urged residents to avoid strenuous outdoor activity, drink water frequently and check on vulnerable neighbors, including older adults, children and people without reliable air conditioning.

“Extreme heat and humidity will significantly increase the potential for heat-related illnesses,” the weather service said in its advisory, warning that conditions could become dangerous quickly for people working or spending time outdoors.

Across Houston, residents said the heat has become impossible to ignore.

“It feels like opening an oven door every time you step outside,” said one Montrose resident, who said she has started walking her dog before sunrise to avoid the worst of the heat. “Even at night, it doesn’t really cool down.”

In the Fifth Ward, a construction worker said crews have been starting earlier in the morning and taking more frequent breaks. “You can’t just push through this kind of heat,” he said. “You have to stop, get shade, drink water — or you’re going to get sick.”

Houston officials have opened cooling centers and encouraged residents without air conditioning to seek relief at libraries, community centers and other public facilities. Public health officials also reminded residents to recognize signs of heat exhaustion, including dizziness, heavy sweating, nausea and weakness. Heat stroke — marked by confusion, fainting or a body temperature above 103 degrees — is a medical emergency, officials said.

The heat is also affecting nearby cities. In **Sugar Land and Pearland**, suburban neighborhoods saw heat index readings well into the triple digits, while officials warned residents to limit outdoor sports and youth practices. In **Galveston**, beachgoers faced oppressive humidity, with little relief from warm Gulf waters and nighttime temperatures staying unusually high. Farther north, **Conroe and The Woodlands** reported dangerous afternoon conditions, while **College Station** also saw record or near-record highs during the same heat wave.

The prolonged heat has placed additional strain on Texas’ electric grid as air conditioners run nearly nonstop. Energy officials have urged conservation during peak demand hours, though no widespread outages were immediately reported in the Houston area.

Meteorologists said a strong ridge of high pressure parked over Texas is responsible for the brutal stretch, suppressing rainfall and allowing temperatures to climb day after day. The lack of overnight cooling has heightened concerns, because the human body has less time to recover from daytime heat stress.

The National Weather Service said relief may be limited in the short term, with above-normal temperatures expected to continue and only isolated rain chances in the forecast.

For many Houstonians, the advice is simple: stay inside, stay hydrated and take the warnings seriously.

“This isn’t just uncomfortable,” one resident said while leaving a grocery store with cases of bottled water. “This is dangerous.”

“This is the kind of heat that wears you down fast,” said **Maria Lopez, a Houston resident**. “Even walking from the parking lot into the grocery store feels exhausting. You can feel it coming off the pavement.”

The heat wave stretched across a broad swath of the central U.S., affecting communities in Texas, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Louisiana, Kansas and Missouri. In many places, overnight temperatures remained unusually warm, offering little relief after sunset and increasing health risks for people whose homes do not cool down.

Emergency officials said heat-related calls typically rise when nighttime temperatures stay elevated because the human body has less opportunity to recover.

In Houston, city officials opened cooling centers and encouraged residents to use libraries, community centers and other public facilities to escape the heat. Outreach teams also checked on vulnerable residents, including people experiencing homelessness.

For outdoor workers, the conditions have been especially punishing.

“People often underestimate heat because it doesn’t look as dramatic as a storm,” said **Dr. Elaine Morris, an emergency physician**. “But extreme heat is one of the deadliest weather hazards. The danger increases when it lasts for several days and nights.”

Meteorologists said the pattern was driven by a strong upper-level ridge of high pressure, sometimes referred to as a “heat dome,” which traps hot air near the surface and suppresses cloud formation and rain. Climate scientists have warned that extreme heat events are becoming more frequent and intense as global temperatures rise, with urban areas such as Houston facing added risk because concrete, asphalt and buildings retain heat.

Relief may be slow to arrive. Forecasts indicated that above-normal temperatures could persist across parts of the central U.S., with only isolated storms offering temporary cooling in some areas.
